prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed GLP-1 first, and I agree that it is the strongest case before us. It is a complete arc from gut-hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1, the active truncated peptide) to a drug class with durable benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism has been confirmed repeatedly by independent groups and the clinical evidence is mature, so recognition is timely. Holst (human physiology and secretion), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, receptor actions, translation) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form) give a three-person prize built on the discovery rather than on industrial development. I prefer a single-achievement prize because the GLP-1 story is already broad and each of the three contributed a different necessary step.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. Habener's early proglucagon and GLP-1 work is not among the supplied names, and the allocation among Mojsov, Habener and others is disputed. Knudsen's decisive long-acting analogue work (liraglutide, semaglutide) is left out, which can read as honouring the physiology while excluding the people who made the drug; including her would need a fourth name. That all six of us ranked it first shows convergence on merit, not that attribution is resolved. I also cannot independently verify the historical priority record from the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but said the credit split between discovery, peptide chemistry and drug development cannot be fully resolved within three names. He placed TOR third and left Sabatini out of his proposal, citing uncertainty about his later history without resting the choice on it.
responses.response: I share the discovery-versus-development concern and resolve it by crediting the physiology and the active peptide, which keeps Knudsen's industrial work outside the prize. I disagree on Sabatini. I included him on TOR because his mTOR nutrient-sensing work extended Hall's and Schreiber's findings, and I would not leave him out on grounds other than the science and the attribution record. TOR is my fourth choice, so this matters less than the GLP-1 question.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked the unfolded protein response second behind GLP-1, calling the Walter and Mori pairing clean and well supported by the supplied credit, and ranked BCL-2 fourth.
responses.response: I agree that Walter and Mori are a compact, well-attributed pair, and clean attribution counts for a lot when GLP-1 and optogenetics are both contested. I still place the UPR below CAR-T and optogenetics because its therapeutic relevance is still developing, and I do not think clean attribution should outweigh demonstrated impact. I would not put it above CAR-T, whose clinical effect is established and whose missing Eshhar credit is a smaller problem than the optogenetics name count.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked CAR-T second and optogenetics third, saying the three-name limit forces hard choices for optogenetics and that Sadelain and June are decisive for CAR-T.
responses.response: I agree that CAR-T is the strongest challenger to GLP-1 and probably the best choice if the committee wants a second part. I put optogenetics second in my opening because it changed experimental biology so broadly, but the six-name credit problem (Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth, Hegemann, Miesenboeck, Nagel) makes it the harder configuration to defend. I also qualify the Rosenberg inclusion. His adoptive cell transfer work is foundational, but I am not sure it belongs in a CAR-specific citation, and the missing Eshhar credit weighs on that trio.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked GLP-1, CAR-T, UPR and optogenetics in that order, treating optogenetics as a widely adopted tool with a difficult three-person cut.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics' impact as a method is not in doubt, but I do not think wide adoption alone makes it a settled prize candidate. A method prize needs a defensible set of laureates, and here the channelrhodopsin discovery (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg) and the neuronal application (Deisseroth, Boyden, Miesenboeck) are separable achievements, which suggests a two-part design if the committee goes that way.

uncertainties: How credit should be divided among Mojsov, Habener, Holst and Drucker for the active GLP-1 peptide and early therapeutic proof of concept.
Whether the committee should recognise the physiology alone or add drug-development contributors such as Knudsen, which would exceed the three-person limit.
If a second part is wanted, whether CAR-T or optogenetics offers the more defensible set of three or fewer people, given the missing Eshhar credit and the six-name optogenetics field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the GLP-1 candidates. I have co-authored with Linnarsson and Frisen and share an institution with several colleagues, but none of this touches B044, B018 or B001; I would flag it if a candidate involving their work came up.
